item.title: authnd, an LDAP server for people who are somewhere else
item.description:
A site’s people are already in a database, a file or another directory. The things that want to authenticate them speak LDAP. authnd is the front: it binds and searches over go-authn/directory’s sources, so what a database holds can be read by anything that knows how to ask a directory. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.11.1, whose entries follow the standard schemas and pass the schema it serves at cn=Subschema, with go-authn/ldap v0.8.0 and go-authn/directory v0.14.0 under it; what is verified and what is not is on the status page.

Upgrading from v0.10.x

  • publish_nt_hash = true now needs a samba block, or authnd does not start.
  • A person without uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory is no longer a posixAccount, and a group without a gidNumber no longer a posixGroup, so a consumer filtering on those classes sees fewer entries: see the entries.
  • A users "ldap" block reads more of the directory behind it by default: see people.

authnd check with the new binary says all three before the restart.

authnd --config /etc/authnd # serve
authnd check /etc/authnd # say what would be served, without listening

The smallest configuration 

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893" # the default
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org" # required

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" }

group "staff" { members = ["alice"] }

People are published as uid=<name>,ou=people,<base_dn>, groups as cn=<name>,ou=groups,<base_dn>. What each entry is follows from what its source gave: a person is an account, or an inetOrgPerson when there is an sn, and a posixAccount only with uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory; every person is a uidObject. A group is a posixGroup (with memberUid) when it has a gidNumber, otherwise a groupOfNames (with member DNs), or an organizationalRole when it is also empty. sshPublicKey is added when the person has keys, and sambaNTPassword when publish_nt_hash says so and a SID can be given. Every entry passes the schema served at cn=Subschema before it is published: see the entries and the schema. Up to v0.10.2 every person was a posixAccount and every group a posixGroup, whatever they had.

--config (-c) takes a file or a directory and may be repeated; a directory is every .hcl file in it, read in name order and merged into one configuration. A configuration with no base_dn, or with nobody in it, does not start.

Who may bind, and who may read

An LDAP server is asked to prove people, so its refusals are the design. These are answers from the v0.10.0 release binary to OpenLDAP’s own client:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin
dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y wrong.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -w ''
ldap_bind: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
additional info: an unauthenticated bind proves nothing, and this server does not accept one
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)'
Insufficient access (50)
Additional information: only a reader may search
request answer why
empty name, empty password (RFC 4513 §5.1.1, anonymous) success it says “I am nobody”, which is true, and a client sends it before it has discovered anything
a name and an empty password (§5.1.2, unauthenticated) unwillingToPerform it names somebody and proves nothing; §5.1.2 asks for exactly this code. invalidCredentials would tell a person their password was wrong
a wrong password, or a name nobody here has invalidCredentials the two are not told apart
a search by anybody but a reader insufficientAccessRights binding proves who you are; reading everybody is a separate thing to be allowed
add, delete, modifyDN unwillingToPerform no handler is wired for them; the one write is a person’s own password

A reader is a service account with a bind DN and password or password_file; a reader with neither is refused at startup (a reader that proves nothing is anonymous search with extra steps). Without any reader, nothing may search, and check says so.

The root DSE is answered to an anonymous client, as discovery needs:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*'
dn:
objectClass: top
objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1
supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3
subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema
vendorName: go-authn/authnd
vendorVersion: v0.11.1

1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1 is the RFC 3062 password modify operation. subschemaSubentry names the schema, which is answered to an anonymous client as well. supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER appears only with an oidc block.

Where to go next

Installing it the release binary, the authnd account, the systemd unit, upgrades
Where the people come from user and group blocks, a SQL database, another LDAP directory
The entries and the schema what each person and group is published as, cn=Subschema, attributes, what is dropped or withheld
check read the configuration back before restarting
TLS ldaps:// or StartTLS, and publish_nt_hash
Changing a password ldappasswd, ldapmodify, and why the old password is always asked for
A Kerberos realm the keytab, and who can be issued a ticket
A second factor a one-time code on the end of the password
A token at the bind OIDC over SASL OAUTHBEARER
Running it signals, restarts, what it logs, how to tell it is up

About the transcripts

Every startup line, the root DSE and the --version lines were printed by the v0.11.1 release binary (authnd-darwin-arm64, go version -m: mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.11.1, vcs.modified=false), and so was every other command shown in the same transcript as a startup line. v0.11.1 changes nothing but that line. Every check table, the entries read back with ldapsearch, cn=Subschema and the samba refusals were printed by the v0.11.0 release binary (mod github.com/go-authn/authnd v0.11.0, vcs.modified=false). So were the configuration refusals on these pages, which v0.11.0 printed byte for byte as v0.10.0 had. The other binds, kinits, password changes and token exchanges were printed by the v0.10.0 release binary and were not run again, since neither v0.11.0’s nor v0.11.1’s release notes change any of them. All of them were asked by the OpenLDAP and Heimdal clients that ship with macOS, on 127.0.0.1 on unprivileged ports, in a scratch directory under /tmp. That is why the configurations behind them name files by relative paths such as etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw, and why the password files have names like alice.pwin. The /etc/authnd paths in the examples are what an installed server uses.

item.title: Installing authnd
item.description:
The repository carries the two files a systemd host needs: packaging/sysusers.d/authnd.conf (the account) and packaging/systemd/authnd.service (the unit). This page explains both and the steps around them. go-pkgx’s versioned services are meant to do this for you later; they do not exist yet.

The release binary

Each tag publishes authnd-<os>-<arch> for linux, darwin and windows on amd64 and arm64 (.exe on windows), built with CGO_ENABLED=0, a SHA256SUMS manifest, and a build provenance attestation for every binary.

version=v0.11.1
arch=amd64 # or arm64
base=https://github.com/go-authn/authnd/releases/download/$version

curl -fsSLO "$base/authnd-linux-$arch"
curl -fsSLO "$base/SHA256SUMS"

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # the bytes the release published
gh attestation verify "authnd-linux-$arch" --repo go-authn/authnd # built by the release workflow, at that tag

Stop if either check fails. The release workflow refuses to publish a binary that does not report exactly the tag it is published under, so the version is something to compare:

$ authnd --version
authnd version v0.11.1

Building only what you want

The server is always there; two build tags leave out where people can come from. -tags nosql drops the three database drivers (PostgreSQL through pgx, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite through modernc.org/sqlite) and the users "sql" block; -tags noldap drops the LDAP client and the users "ldap" block. A configuration naming a block the binary was built without is told so — this binary was built without SQL support (-tags nosql) — rather than that the block does not exist. The release binaries are built without tags.

The account 

#Type Name ID Description Home Shell
u authnd - "authnd LDAP directory and Kerberos KDC" /var/lib/authnd -

A static account from sysusers.d, not DynamicUser=. The files authnd reads — password files, a DSN, a keytab, a TLS key — are secrets given to the authnd group ahead of time, and a password change writes back into them. A dynamic uid does not exist until the service starts, and a file it wrote would belong to a number that later means somebody else.

The two files come from the packaging/ directory of the release tag, the same version as the binary: copy that directory beside the binary, from a checkout of the tag or, for v0.11.1, from https://github.com/go-authn/authnd/tree/v0.11.1/packaging.

sudo install -m 0755 "authnd-linux-$arch" /usr/local/bin/authnd
sudo install -m 0644 packaging/sysusers.d/authnd.conf /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf
sudo systemd-sysusers /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf
sudo install -m 0644 packaging/systemd/authnd.service /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service
sudo systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

What the unit grants, and why 

[Service]
Type=exec
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/authnd --config /etc/authnd
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s

User=authnd
Group=authnd
UMask=0077

AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes

StateDirectory=authnd
StateDirectoryMode=0700

ProtectSystem=strict

The rest of the unit is the usual hardening (ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, ProtectProc=invisible, the kernel and cgroup protections, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, SystemCallFilter=@system-service, RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX). Three things it leaves out are deliberate:
ExecReload= authnd has no reload. It reads its configuration, certificate and keytab once; see running it
PrivateUsers= inside a user namespace CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE no longer applies to the host’s network, and the bind to 389 is refused
ProcSubset=pid it hides /proc/sys, where Go reads net/core/somaxconn, and every listener’s backlog falls to Go’s fallback of 128

IPAddressAllow=/IPAddressDeny= are not set either: which networks may ask a directory is the site’s to say, in a drop-in:

sudo systemctl edit authnd
[Service]
IPAddressDeny=any
IPAddressAllow=localhost 10.0.0.0/8

The one capability is for the privileged ports: LDAP 389, LDAPS 636, and Kerberos 88 over UDP and TCP. A PostgreSQL or MariaDB on the same machine is reached through its socket, which a read-only file system allows. The state directory, /var/lib/authnd, is there for a SQLite database; authnd keeps no state of its own — the second-factor lockout counts live in memory and are reset at every restart.

The configuration directory 

sudo install -d -o root -g authnd -m 0750 /etc/authnd

Every file inside it root:authnd, mode 0640. Secrets go in files named by *_file keys rather than inline: a file has permissions, and a configuration someone pastes does not. With ProtectSystem=strict the service cannot write under /etc, which is right for the configuration and wrong for the passwords people change themselves — give those a directory of their own:

sudo install -d -o authnd -g authnd -m 0700 /etc/authnd/passwords
sudo systemctl edit authnd
[Service]
ReadWritePaths=/etc/authnd/passwords

Why that directory and not the file is explained in changing a password.

key default
base_dn — (required) the root of the tree, e.g. dc=example,dc=org; a value with no = is refused
listen 127.0.0.1:3893 one address. Loopback by default: a directory that appears on every interface the moment it starts is a decision somebody should make on purpose. A site that needs LDAP and LDAPS runs two instances
reader "<dn>" none a service account that may search; see who may read
cert_file, key_file, starttls, publish_nt_hash, samba off TLS
user, group, users — the people; at least one user or users block
kerberos none a realm
mfa none a second factor
oidc none a token at the bind

A relative path in the configuration is resolved against the directory the process runs in, not the configuration file’s; the unit runs from /, so write paths absolute.

Before every start:

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd
sudo systemctl enable --now authnd
journalctl -u authnd

check is described on its own page; running it as authnd also proves the account can read every file.

Upgrade, roll back, remove

Check the configuration with the new binary before it replaces the old one, and keep the old one. The new binary is installed beside the old one first: that makes it executable, and puts it where the authnd account can run it.

sudo install -m 0755 "authnd-linux-$arch" /usr/local/bin/authnd.new
sudo -u authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.new check /etc/authnd
sudo cp /usr/local/bin/authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.previous
sudo mv /usr/local/bin/authnd.new /usr/local/bin/authnd
sudo systemctl restart authnd
authnd --version

Compare packaging/ at the new tag with what is installed (v0.11.1’s is v0.10.2’s, unchanged). Rolling back is the same install from authnd.previous, and a restart.

From v0.10.x to v0.11.0 the check above is the step that matters: a configuration with publish_nt_hash = true and no samba block is refused there rather than at the restart, and the lines after its tables say who is no longer a posixAccount and which groups are no longer posixGroups (the entries).

To remove it:

sudo systemctl disable --now authnd
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service
sudo rm -r /etc/systemd/system/authnd.service.d # if a drop-in was added
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/authnd /usr/local/bin/authnd.previous /usr/lib/sysusers.d/authnd.conf

/etc/authnd, /var/lib/authnd and the authnd account are left in place: the first two hold people’s credentials, and a uid that is reused can be given somebody else’s files. Remove them deliberately.

item.title: Where the people come from
item.description:
A user block is the whole directory for a small site, or the service accounts a big one keeps out of its database. A site whose people are already in a database or in LDAP should not copy them into a second place that goes stale, so a users block reads them where they are. The users block is go-authn/directory’s hcldir, the same one go-fileshare reads: one directory is described the same way to both.

Written in the configuration 

user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" }

user "carol" {
 nt_hash = "…" # MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex
 authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… carol@laptop"] # published as sshPublicKey
}

group "staff" { members = ["alice", "carol"] }
field what it is
password the password, inline
password_file the same, read from a file (surrounding white space removed)
nt_hash MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex characters — for a site that holds that and not the password
totp_secret a base32 one-time-code secret, at least 128 bits; see a second factor
authorized_keys authorized_keys lines, published as sshPublicKey
authorized_keys_file the same, from a file
attributes from v0.11.0, what describes the person and proves nothing — sn, uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, mail… — as a map of strings or lists of strings; a group block takes it too. They decide what the entry is published as: see the entries

Refused at startup, naming the person:

  • password and password_file together — say which one;
  • password and nt_hash together — the hash is derived from the password, so two of them can disagree;
  • authorized_keys and authorized_keys_file together;
  • an nt_hash that is not 32 hex characters, an authorized_keys line that does not parse, a totp_secret under 128 bits;
  • the same user or group twice, and a group with no members.

A group member that no source knows is refused too, which is what catches a typo before it silently grants nothing:

$ authnd check cases/typo.hcl
authnd: group "staff" has "alise" in it, who is not in the configuration file

An nt_hash alone cannot bind

A person written with only nt_hash is published, can be handed to an SMB server through sambaNTPassword, and cannot bind to authnd itself: an LDAP simple bind sends the password, and an NT hash is not a way to check one here. bob below has only an NT hash, and the hash is that of the password sent:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y bob.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)

check says so, after the tables:

bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against

In a SQL database 

users "sql" {
 driver = "postgres" # or mysql (mariadb), or sqlite
 dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/pg.dsn" # required: a DSN may hold a password
 users = "select login, secret, nt_hash from staff" # required
 groups = "select team, member from team_members" # optional
}

The queries are yours, because a site’s people are already in that site’s shape. The users query’s columns are read by position: a name, then any of a password, an NT hash, SSH keys (one per line) and a one-time-code secret, in that order — up to five columns. A NULL is a credential that person does not have. A password column is compared as it is stored: authnd has no setting for a hashed column. The groups query returns a group name and a member, one row per membership.

Two more queries, optional, read attributes by column alias rather than by position: users_attributes (a name, then one column per attribute) and groups_attributes (a group, then the same). An unquoted alias is lower-cased by PostgreSQL. See the entries.

driver accepts postgres (or postgresql, pgx), mysql (or mariadb) and sqlite (or sqlite3). The database is reached at startup, before anything listens, so one that is not answering stops the server where somebody is watching:

$ authnd check cases/nodb
authnd: users "sql": the postgres database is not answering: failed to connect to `user=authnd database=authnd`:
127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused
127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

PostgreSQL on the same machine through its socket and peer authentication needs no password in the DSN: host=/run/postgresql dbname=authnd user=authnd. SQLite in the state directory: file:/var/lib/authnd/people.db.

A key that belongs to the other kind of block is refused rather than ignored:

$ authnd check cases/sqlwrongkey.hcl
authnd: users "sql" has base_dn in it, which belongs to an ldap block

In another LDAP directory 

users "ldap" {
 url = "ldaps://ldap.example.org"
 base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_password_file = "/etc/authnd/upstream.pw"
}

url and base_dn are required. Where the people and groups are, and which attributes name them:

key default
user_filter (|(objectClass=posixAccount)(objectClass=account)(objectClass=uidObject))
user_attribute uid
group_base_dn base_dn
group_filter (|(objectClass=posixGroup)(objectClass=groupOfNames))
group_attribute cn
group_member_attribute none: memberUid (names) and member (DNs); set, it is the one attribute read
totp_attribute none: there is no standard attribute, and a guess would read nothing while looking like it had looked
attributes, group_attributes none: the attributes to copy from each person’s entry and each group’s, such as ["mail", "uidNumber", "homeDirectory"] and ["gidNumber"] (the entries)
start_tls false

A member DN counts only when it is the DN of an entry the people search returned: a DN outside them, or naming nobody, maps to nobody, and the name is never read out of the DN. sambaNTPassword and sshPublicKey are read under those names.

From v0.11.0 the defaults read more of an institution’s directory

The block is go-authn/directory’s, and directory v0.14.0, which authnd v0.11.0 embeds, widened its defaults: up to v0.10.2, user_filter was (objectClass=posixAccount), group_filter (objectClass=posixGroup) and group_member_attribute memberUid. A directory holding account or uidObject entries that are not posixAccounts — service accounts, hosts named by uid, people imported from elsewhere — now gives them to authnd, and each can be checked by a bind; its groupOfNames groups become groups here. To keep exactly the old set, write the old values:

users "ldap" {
 # ...
 user_filter = "(objectClass=posixAccount)"
 group_filter = "(objectClass=posixGroup)"
 group_member_attribute = "memberUid"
}

Two things are refused before anything is opened:

$ authnd check cases/ldap-clear.hcl
authnd: users "ldap" would send every password to "ldap.example.org" in the clear: use ldaps://, or start_tls = true (RFC 4513 §5.1.3)
$ authnd check cases/ldap-cred.hcl
authnd: users "ldap" has credentials in its url, and a url is printed: use bind_dn with bind_password_file

ldap:// to a loopback address and ldapi:// are accepted: nobody is on the way.

A directory behind this one checks passwords by binding to it; it does not hand them over. Here one authnd fronts another, under a different base; the one behind is the check example, served on 3893:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3894"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=net"

users "ldap" {
 url = "ldap://127.0.0.1:3893"
 base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
 group_base_dn = "ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw"
}

user "svc-backup" { password_file = "etc/authnd/svc-backup.pw" }
$ authnd check front2
ldap://127.0.0.1:3894, base dc=example,dc=net
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
bob ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
dora ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
eli ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check account, uidObject uid
svc-backup the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
engineers dora and eli groupOfNames
staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
svc-backup has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group engineers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
a bind carries a password
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

Every person the directory behind publishes is an account and every group a groupOfNames, since none has POSIX attributes: the defaults read them, and the groups’ member DNs map to the people imported. With the defaults up to v0.10.2, (objectClass=posixAccount) would have matched none of them.

A password check is enough for a bind, and is never enough for a Kerberos ticket or for SMB.

Order, and the one exception

Sources are asked in the order they are written, and the first one that knows a name owns it. The user blocks always come first, so a service account written down locally is not overridden by somebody with the same name in the database. Group membership is the union of every source: a group that a group block and a database’s groups query both name has the members of both.

Two names that differ only by case are refused

A uid is compared ignoring case (RFC 4519 §2.39), and so is every DN, so Dora in the file and dora in a database are one name to LDAP and two people to anything that compares bytes — a password change by one would land on the other. Such a configuration does not start:

$ authnd check cases/case.hcl
authnd: "Dora" (from the configuration file) and "dora" (from a sqlite database) differ only by case, and an LDAP name does not tell them apart: a uid is compared ignoring case. Rename one of them

Read once

Every source is read once, at startup. A person added to the database, or a membership changed in the directory behind this one, is served after a restart, not before. That includes a password column in a database: it is read with the rest of the row. A directory behind this one is different only in that a bind is checked by binding to it, so a password changed there is the one that works. The other exception is a password a person changes through authnd itself, which is applied at once. There is no reload; see running it.

item.title: The entries authnd publishes, and the schema it serves
item.description:
Every entry authnd publishes passes the schema it serves. From v0.11.0 each person and group is a standard-schema entry, built from what its source gave, and checked with go-authn/ldap’s schema.Validate against the schema a client can read at cn=Subschema before it is ever returned by a search. A client that reads the schema and believes it — an LDAP browser, a synchronisation tool, a directory replicating this one — is shown what it was told. Up to v0.10.2 every person was top, person, posixAccount with none of the attributes those classes require, and sambaNTPassword sat on an entry with no class that allows it.

A consumer filtering on posixAccount or posixGroup sees fewer entries

A person without uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory is no longer a posixAccount, and a group without a gidNumber is no longer a posixGroup. A program that searches (objectClass=posixAccount) or (objectClass=posixGroup) no longer finds them. That includes go-authn/directory’s ldapdir up to v0.13.0, and so go-fileshare until it requires directory v0.14.0, whose defaults also read account, uidObject and groupOfNames (directory). Give people and groups those attributes, or point the consumer at (objectClass=uidObject), which every person carries.

The shapes

Every superclass is listed, as RFC 4512 §3.3 asks.

a person with… objectClass cn
no sn top, account (RFC 4524 §3.1) only when another class allows it
sn top, person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson (RFC 4519, RFC 2798) yes
… and uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, all three + posixAccount (RFC 2307) yes
… and SSH keys + ldapPublicKey (openssh-lpk), with sshPublicKey
… and a published NT hash with a sambaSID + sambaSamAccount (Samba), with sambaSID and sambaNTPassword: see the samba block allowed
… always + uidObject (RFC 4519 §3.14), so (objectClass=uidObject) finds everybody
a group with… objectClass members
a gidNumber top, posixGroup (RFC 2307) memberUid, names
no gidNumber, somebody in it top, groupOfNames (RFC 4519 §3.5) member, the DNs this server publishes
no gidNumber, nobody in it top, organizationalRole (RFC 4519 §3.10) none
a gidNumber, nobody in it top, posixGroup none: an attribute has at least one value

uid is the person’s name, and so is cn wherever a class allows it. An account alone does not allow cn (its MAY is description, seeAlso, l, o, ou and host), so a person without sn and without the POSIX trio carries uid and no cn.

Why these choices, from authnd’s own reasons:

  • posixGroup follows RFC 2307, not draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02. The draft makes posixGroup AUXILIARY and expired unpublished; an AUXILIARY posixGroup would need a structural class beside it, groupOfNames, whose member an empty group cannot give.
  • organizationalRole for an empty group without a gidNumber. groupOfNames and groupOfUniqueNames both require a member, and the ways of inventing one are false: member: "" names the root DSE, and the group’s own DN makes it a member of itself. organizationalRole is the one standard structural class whose only MUST is cn, and it takes description, ou and seeAlso as groupOfNames does.
  • Auxiliary classes without DIT content rules. RFC 4512 §2.4.3 forbids auxiliary classes on an entry whose structural class has no DIT content rule. Every directory server in use allows them, and so does Validate.

Adding attributes

What a source says about somebody that proves nothing — a uidNumber, a home directory, a mail address — is an attribute, published as given. They are go-authn/directory’s attributes, from v0.13.0, and they are kept apart from credentials: a name that holds a secret, or one the server derives itself, is refused before anything is read.

In a user or group block 

user "dora" {
 password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/dora.pw"
 authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… dora@laptop"]
 attributes = {
 sn = "Explorer" # inetOrgPerson
 uidNumber = "1000" # the three: posixAccount
 gidNumber = "1000"
 homeDirectory = "/home/dora"
 mail = ["dora@example.org", "d.explorer@example.org"]
 }
}

group "engineers" {
 members = ["dora", "eli"]
 attributes = { gidNumber = "2000" } # a posixGroup; without it, a groupOfNames
}

A value is a string or a list of strings; null leaves the attribute out. A number is refused, because an LDAP value is a string and authnd does not choose how a number is spelled:

$ authnd check cases/number.hcl
authnd: user "alice": attributes: uidNumber is the number 1000: write it as a string, "1000" -- an LDAP value is a string, and this does not choose how a number is spelled
$ authnd check cases/secret.hcl
authnd: user "alice": attributes: directory: not an attribute this package carries: "userPassword" holds a secret, and attributes are published: a credential has its own option or none

Refused the same way, whatever their case: any name holding a secret (userPassword, sambaNTPassword, unicodePwd, krbPrincipalKey and the rest of go-authn/directory’s list, or any name containing password, passwd, pwd, secret, credential, hash or privatekey); sshPublicKey, which has authorized_keys; uid, cn and objectClass, which the server derives; member, memberUid and the other membership attributes, which members answers; the operational attributes a server maintains; and a name in numeric form (2.5.4.35 is userPassword).

In a SQL database

Two optional queries of a users "sql" block read attributes by column alias. The first column is the person’s or the group’s name; every other column is an attribute named by its alias:

users "sql" {
 driver = "sqlite"
 dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/people.dsn"
 users = "select login, secret, null, ssh_keys from staff"
 groups = "select team, member from teams"
 users_attributes = "select login, sn, uid as uidNumber, gid as gidNumber, home as homeDirectory, mail from person_attrs"
 groups_attributes = "select team, gid as gidNumber, description from team_attrs"
}
  • The positional users and groups queries are unchanged, and a sixth positional column is still refused: attributes come by name, in their own query.
  • A column whose alias is not an attribute description (an unaliased expression such as count(*)), or names a credential, is refused with its column number before a row is read.
  • NULL and '' are absent. A name may come back on several rows, and the values of all of them are kept, so a join to a table of addresses gives a person several.
  • A group named only in groups_attributes exists, with nobody in it: that is how a person’s own primary group is written.

The case of an alias is the database’s

PostgreSQL folds an unquoted alias to lower case: as uidNumber comes back as uidnumber. Attribute names are case-insensitive, so it is the same attribute and the entry is the same entry to every LDAP client, but the spelling authnd prints is the database’s. Quote the alias where the spelling matters: gid as "gidNumber". SQLite keeps an alias as written.

From another LDAP directory

A users "ldap" block copies the attributes it is told to, from each person’s entry and each group’s: attributes = ["mail", "uidNumber", "homeDirectory"] and group_attributes = ["gidNumber"]. See people.

A configuration, and what it publishes

The SQL block above, with a reader, over a SQLite database of five people and four groups, as the v0.11.0 release binary checks it:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org"

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

users "sql" {
 driver = "sqlite"
 dsn_file = "etc/authnd/people.dsn"
 users = "select login, secret, null, ssh_keys from staff"
 groups = "select team, member from teams"
 users_attributes = "select login, sn, uid as uidNumber, gid as gidNumber, home as homeDirectory, mail from person_attrs"
 groups_attributes = "select team, gid as gidNumber, description from team_attrs"
}
$ authnd check etc/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
dora a sqlite database a password and 1 key person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, posixAccount, ldapPublicKey, uidObject uid, cn, sn, uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory, mail and sshPublicKey
eli a sqlite database a password account, posixAccount, uidObject uid, cn, uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory
fay a sqlite database a password person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject uid, cn, sn and mail
gus a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
hal a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
alumni nobody organizationalRole
engineers dora and eli posixGroup
nobody-yet nobody posixGroup
readers fay and gus groupOfNames
fay has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as person, organizationalPerson, inetOrgPerson, uidObject
gus has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
hal has no homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
hal is published without uidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would
hal is published without gidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount and posixGroup would
hal is published without mail: no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would
group alumni has no gidNumber and nobody in it: not a posixGroup, published as an organizationalRole (a groupOfNames needs a member)
group readers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
a bind carries a password
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

PUBLISHED AS is each entry’s object classes, without top, and WITH its attributes, read off the entries a search returns. hal has a uidNumber, a gidNumber and a mail and no homeDirectory or sn: hal is an account, which allows none of the three, so they are dropped and the rest is published. The server says the same at startup (and stopping when it was stopped):

$ authnd --config etc/authnd
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 5 people from a sqlite database
uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without uidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would
uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without gidNumber: no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount and posixGroup would
uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without mail: no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would
stopping

Read back by OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch, with the reader’s password in a file:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(|(uid=dora)(uid=eli)(uid=gus)(uid=hal))'
dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: person
objectClass: organizationalPerson
objectClass: inetOrgPerson
objectClass: posixAccount
objectClass: ldapPublicKey
objectClass: uidObject
uid: dora
cn: dora
sn: Explorer
uidNumber: 1000
gidNumber: 1000
homeDirectory: /home/dora
mail: dora@example.org
sshPublicKey: ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIKTfVR7FqXWE/0VEcjrUhK+Fz/MLqlwGPIxalr6onRMn dora@laptop
dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: posixAccount
objectClass: uidObject
uid: eli
cn: eli
uidNumber: 1001
gidNumber: 1001
homeDirectory: /home/eli
dn: uid=gus,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: uidObject
uid: gus
dn: uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: uidObject
uid: hal
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=*)'
dn: cn=alumni,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: organizationalRole
cn: alumni
description: people who were here
dn: cn=engineers,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: posixGroup
cn: engineers
gidNumber: 2000
memberUid: dora
memberUid: eli
dn: cn=nobody-yet,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: posixGroup
cn: nobody-yet
gidNumber: 2001
dn: cn=readers,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: groupOfNames
cn: readers
description: people who read
member: uid=fay,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
member: uid=gus,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org

alumni is named only in groups_attributes, so it exists with nobody in it; without a gidNumber it is an organizationalRole. nobody-yet has a gidNumber and nobody, so it is a posixGroup without memberUid.

Which class finds whom:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=uidObject)' 1.1
dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
dn: uid=fay,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
dn: uid=gus,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
dn: uid=hal,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(objectClass=posixAccount)' 1.1
dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org

What is dropped, and what is withheld

given the entry why
uidNumber, gidNumber, no homeDirectory, no sn account, uidObject, without the two no class of the entry allows it; posixAccount would
mail, no sn account, uidObject, without it no class of the entry allows it; inetOrgPerson would
a type the schema does not define the rest the schema served here does not define it
mail on a group without a gidNumber groupOfNames, without it
two homeDirectory values with the POSIX trio withheld: SINGLE-VALUE, nothing to drop
a gidNumber that is not an integer withheld: not of its syntax

Only what a source gave is dropped, and which attribute is not allowed is Validate’s answer, not a second reading of the schema. The entry is validated again after dropping. An entry that still fails is withheld: it is absent from every search, the startup log names it, and check lists it with every problem Validate found. An attribute authnd derives itself (uid, cn, objectClass, sshPublicKey, sambaSID, sambaNTPassword) that the schema refused would be a defect in authnd, and withholds the entry rather than publish it without.

alice’s gidNumber is a word here:

listen = "127.0.0.1:3893"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org"

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

user "alice" {
 password_file = "etc/authnd/alice.pw"
 attributes = {
 uidNumber = "1000"
 gidNumber = "staff"
 homeDirectory = "/home/alice"
 }
}

user "bob" { password_file = "etc/authnd/bob.pw" }
$ authnd check cases/withheld.hcl
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password NOT PUBLISHED (see below) uid, cn, gidNumber, homeDirectory and uidNumber
bob the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
alice is NOT published: as account, posixAccount, uidObject it fails the schema:
- the value "staff" of gidNumber is not of its syntax 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27
a bind carries a password
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

Served, alice can still bind and is in no search, and the server says why at startup:

$ authnd --config cases/withheld.hcl
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 2 people from the configuration file
uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is NOT published: it fails the schema: the value "staff" of gidNumber is not of its syntax 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin
dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)'

What is withheld is the entry a search returns, not the identity.

The schema it serves

The root DSE names it (subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema, on the root DSE), and a base search of cn=Subschema returns it (RFC 4512 §4.2): the standard definitions go-authn/ldap embeds — RFC 4512, 4517, 4519, 4523, 4524, 2798, 2307, 3672 and 3045, and openssh-lpk — plus Samba’s sambaSamAccount, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword when there is a samba block. The definitions are published only when asked for by name or with +. Trimmed where marked:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -s base -b cn=Subschema '+' '*'
dn: cn=Subschema
objectClass: top
objectClass: subentry
objectClass: subschema
cn: Subschema
subtreeSpecification: {}
ldapSyntaxes: ( 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.3 DESC 'Attribute Type Description' )
[...]
matchingRules: ( 2.5.13.15 NAME 'integerOrderingMatch' SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 )
[...]
attributeTypes: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.1.0 NAME 'uidNumber' DESC 'An integer uniquely identifying a user in an administrative domain' EQUALITY integerMatch ORDERING integerOrderingMatch SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 SINGLE-VALUE )
attributeTypes: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.1.1 NAME 'gidNumber' DESC 'An integer uniquely identifying a group in an administrative domain' EQUALITY integerMatch ORDERING integerOrderingMatch SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.27 SINGLE-VALUE )
[...]
objectClasses: ( 2.5.6.9 NAME 'groupOfNames' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST ( member $ cn ) MAY ( businessCategory $ seeAlso $ owner $ ou $ o $ description ) )
[...]
objectClasses: ( 1.3.6.1.1.3.1 NAME 'uidObject' SUP top AUXILIARY MUST uid )
objectClasses: ( 0.9.2342.19200300.100.4.5 NAME 'account' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST uid MAY ( description $ seeAlso $ l $ o $ ou $ host ) )
[...]
objectClasses: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.2.0 NAME 'posixAccount' DESC 'Abstraction of an account with POSIX attributes' SUP top AUXILIARY MUST ( cn $ uid $ uidNumber $ gidNumber $ homeDirectory ) MAY ( userPassword $ loginShell $ gecos $ description ) )
[...]
objectClasses: ( 1.3.6.1.1.1.2.2 NAME 'posixGroup' DESC 'Abstraction of a group of accounts' SUP top STRUCTURAL MUST ( cn $ gidNumber ) MAY ( userPassword $ memberUid $ description ) )
[...]

The whole entry was 327 lines: 49 syntaxes, 40 matching rules, 36 matching rule uses, 143 attribute types and 52 object classes. Unlike a search under the base, the subschema entry, like the root DSE, is answered to an anonymous client: the same query without -D and -y returned it.

Filters use the schema’s matching rules, so (uidNumber>=1000) compares integers. uidNumber and gidNumber have ORDERING integerOrderingMatch, which RFC 2307 does not give them; slapd and draft-howard-rfc2307bis-02 do, and so does go-authn/ldap (its one departure). As strings, 1000 sorts before 999:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uidNumber>=1000)' uidNumber
dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
uidNumber: 1000
dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
uidNumber: 1001
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b dc=example,dc=org '(uidNumber>=999)' uidNumber
dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
uidNumber: 1000
dn: uid=eli,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
uidNumber: 1001

hal is not there: hal’s uidNumber was dropped. A range on an attribute with no ORDERING rule, such as uid, is Undefined and matches nothing.

item.title: check, before you restart something people log in through
item.description:
authnd check /etc/authnd
authnd check --config a.hcl --config b.hcl

check reads the configuration exactly as the server does, opens everything the server opens before it listens — the files, the database, the directory behind this one, the identity provider’s discovery document, the TLS certificate and key, the keytab — and prints what would be published and to whom, without listening. It prints where every credential comes from and never what is in it. It exits 0 and ends with this configuration can be served, or exits 1 with the one sentence that stops the server.

A configuration that can be served

Two user blocks, a reader, and a SQLite database, in a directory of two files (authnd.hcl and people.hcl):

$ authnd check etc/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid
dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
engineers dora and eli groupOfNames
staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group engineers has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
a bind carries a password
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

Reading it

The first line is the scheme, the address and the base: ldap://, ldaps://, or ldap+starttls:// — see TLS.

column
FROM the source that owns the name: the configuration file, a sqlite database (or postgres, mysql), or the url of a directory behind this one
CAN PROVE a password (held, so it can be compared and keys derived from it), a password check (another directory answers yes or no), an NT hash, N keys, a one-time-code secret, or nothing
PUBLISHED AS the entry’s object classes, without top, as the shapes give them — or NOT PUBLISHED (see below) for an entry that fails the schema
WITH the attributes the entry carries, read off the entry a search returns: uid; cn wherever a class allows it; what the sources gave, less what was dropped; sshPublicKey when there are keys; sambaSID and sambaNTPassword when publish_nt_hash is on and the person has an NT key and a SID

The group table has a PUBLISHED AS column too: posixGroup, groupOfNames or organizationalRole. Up to v0.10.2, PUBLISHED AS was the list of attributes, uid and cn for nearly everybody, and there was no WITH column.

The lines after the tables say what a person needs to know before relying on the configuration. First, about the entries:

  • who is not a posixAccount, and which of uidNumber, gidNumber and homeDirectory they lack;
  • which groups have no gidNumber, and what they are published as instead;
  • every attribute dropped because no class of its entry allows it, and which classes would;
  • every entry not published, with each problem the schema check found;
  • who has an NT key and no sambaSID, and so no sambaNTPassword.

Then, about binds and searches:

  • what a bind carries: a password, or, with an mfa block, a password with a 6-digit code after it; with an oidc block, where tokens come from and over what;
  • who cannot bind with a password at all: people known only by an NT hash — see people;
  • who may search: the readers, or no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected;
  • whether sambaNTPassword is published, and over what — see publish_nt_hash;
  • with a kerberos block, the realm and who can and who cannot be issued a ticket, with the reason;
  • with an mfa block, who has no second factor, and so cannot bind with a password; with an oidc block beside it the line adds that a token whose amr names two kinds still can;
  • a group that names somebody no source has.

That last one is published as it stands — a front for one system legitimately carries names another one owns — but it is said, because the other reading is a typo. In a posixGroup the stranger is a memberUid; in a groupOfNames it is a member DN that names no entry here, member: uid=zoe,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org here, which go-authn/directory’s ldapdir from v0.14.0 maps to nobody. Here the database’s team_members table has a row for zoe, who is nobody here:

GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
engineers dora, eli and zoe groupOfNames
staff alice, bob and dora groupOfNames
[...]
engineers names zoe, who has no entry here: the group is published as it stands, and nothing here can prove them

(A group block naming a stranger is refused outright; see people.)

What it refuses

Each of these stops check and the server alike, with exit status 1. They are on the pages where they belong; a few, as printed:

$ authnd check cases/nobody.hcl
authnd: there is nobody here: name a user, or a users block reading a database or a directory
$ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear
$ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl
authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks
$ authnd check empty
authnd: empty has no .hcl files in it
$ authnd
authnd: no configuration: give a .hcl file or a directory of them

The certificate, the keytab, and the one thing it cannot see

A certificate that does not load and a keytab without krbtgt/REALM are refused by check, in the words the server would use:

$ authnd check cases/badcert
authnd: the certificate: open tls/missing.pem: no such file or directory
$ authnd check cases/nokrbtgt
authnd: kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG" realm: EXAMPLE.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18

What check cannot know without listening is whether the ports are free. A second server on the same Kerberos address passes check and is refused at start:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

Run it as the service account 

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd

so that a file only root can read fails here, not at the restart. Run it with the new binary before an upgrade; see install.

item.title: TLS: ldaps:// or StartTLS, and not both at once
item.description:
listen = "0.0.0.0:636"
cert_file = "/etc/authnd/cert.pem" # the chain, leaf first
key_file = "/etc/authnd/key.pem"

cert_file and key_file together turn TLS on; one without the other is refused (one without the other serves nothing). TLS 1.2 is the minimum. authnd has no ACME client: the two files are written by something else — go-authn/servercert, certbot, a site’s own CA — and authnd is restarted after each renewal, because the certificate is read once, when the listener opens.

Two ways, one listener each

starttls the listener check says
ldaps:// not set the TLS handshake happens before a byte of LDAP is spoken ldaps://…
StartTLS starttls = true plaintext, upgraded when the client asks (RFC 4511 §4.14) ldap+starttls://…

It is one or the other and has to be: a listener cannot both require a handshake and wait to see whether one is asked for. Which one a site wants is about its clients: ldaps:// on 636 is what most of them are configured for, and StartTLS is what a client pointed at 389 with “use TLS” ticked will ask for. A site that needs both runs two instances, each with its own --config. starttls = true without a certificate is refused:

$ authnd check cases/starttls-nocert.hcl
authnd: starttls needs cert_file and key_file: there is nothing to upgrade a connection WITH

ldaps://

The server, a CA-signed certificate for 127.0.0.1, and the chain verified by a client that is not this program:

$ authnd --config ldaps
ldaps on 127.0.0.1:3636, serving 3 people from the configuration file
uid=carol,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org is published without sambaNTPassword: no sambaSID and no uidNumber to derive one from
$ openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:3636 -CAfile tls/ca.pem -verify_return_error -verify_ip 127.0.0.1 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify return|Protocol|subject=|issuer='
subject=CN=localhost
issuer=CN=docs test CA
Protocol: TLSv1.3
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
Protocol : TLSv1.3
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

StartTLS, which refuses until it is asked for

StartTLS is requested by the client, so merely offering it promises nothing: a client that never asks would bind in the clear. A listener with starttls = true therefore refuses every bind and every search until the connection has been upgraded, with confidentialityRequired:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=bob)'
ldap_bind: Confidentiality required (13)
additional info: this listener requires TLS, and nothing asked for it
$ LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never ldapsearch -ZZ -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=bob)'
dn: uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: sambaSamAccount
objectClass: uidObject
uid: bob
cn: bob
sambaSID: S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-1104
sambaNTPassword: 8846F7EAEE8FB117AD06BDD830B7586C

(-ZZ is “StartTLS, and fail if it fails”. LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never is there because the ldapsearch macOS ships trusts the system store and could not be told to trust this test CA; the chain was checked separately with openssl s_client -starttls ldap -CAfile tls/ca.pem -verify_return_error, which answered Verify return code: 0 (ok).)

That refusal is what makes cert_file a guarantee rather than an offer — and it is what publish_nt_hash relies on. It includes the anonymous bind ldapsearch -x sends before reading the root DSE, so on a StartTLS listener that discovery query, too, needs -ZZ.

publish_nt_hash

sambaNTPassword is what lets a Samba or another SMB server authenticate people through this directory, and it is not a password hash in the sense a login form means: whoever holds MD4(UTF16LE(password)) authenticates as that person over NTLMv2 without ever learning the password. So it is published only when asked for, and, from v0.11.0, with the domain the people’s SIDs belong to:

publish_nt_hash = true
samba {
 domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330" # `net getlocalsid` on the SMB server
}

Asking for it is refused unless the listener has TLS, or is loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost) and so on no network at all:

$ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear

The samba block

sambaNTPassword belongs to Samba’s sambaSamAccount, whose MUST is uid and sambaSID, and no other class allows it. Every entry authnd publishes passes the schema it serves, so the attribute is published only on a sambaSamAccount, and that needs a SID:

key
domain_sid required: the SMB server’s domain SID, S-1-5-21-…, as net getlocalsid prints it
algorithmic_rid_base optional, 1000 by default, Samba’s. An odd number, or one below 1000, is refused: Samba would silently use another one

A person’s sambaSID is their own sambaSID attribute when a source gives one (attributes). Otherwise it is domain_sid-RID, with RID = 2 × uidNumber + algorithmic_rid_base: Samba’s algorithmic mapping (smb.conf(5), algorithmic rid base). A person with an NT key and neither is published without sambaNTPassword, and check and the startup log say who. The Samba definitions are added to the schema served at cn=Subschema only when the block is there; they were written from Samba’s published OIDs, names and syntaxes, not copied from its GPL-3.0 samba.schema.

Breaking for v0.10.x configurations: publish_nt_hash without a samba block does not start

v0.10.x served publish_nt_hash = true alone. From v0.11.0 that configuration is refused at startup and by check, with what to add:

$ authnd check cases/nthash.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs a samba block: sambaNTPassword belongs to Samba's sambaSamAccount, whose MUST is uid and sambaSID, and a SID needs the domain's. Add
samba {
domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-..." # the SMB server's: `net getlocalsid` prints it
}
and each person's sambaSID is their own sambaSID attribute, or domain_sid-(2 x uidNumber + 1000), Samba's algorithmic mapping; `authnd check` lists who has neither

Run check with the new binary before upgrading. Refusing is deliberate: the v0.10.x entry cannot pass the schema, and the two quiet alternatives — dropping the attribute, which takes SMB away from everybody, or dropping the entry, which takes the person away — would both happen with nothing on the console.

A samba block without publish_nt_hash is refused too, since it would publish nothing:

$ authnd check cases/samba-alone.hcl
authnd: a samba block without publish_nt_hash publishes nothing: it is the domain of the sambaSID that sambaNTPassword needs. Remove it, or set publish_nt_hash = true

What check says

Three people on an ldaps:// listener: alice has a password and the POSIX trio, so their SID is derived (2 × 1000 + 1000); bob has only an NT hash and a sambaSID of their own; carol has a password and neither.

listen = "127.0.0.1:3636"
base_dn = "dc=example,dc=org"
cert_file = "tls/cert.pem"
key_file = "tls/key.pem"

publish_nt_hash = true
samba {
 domain_sid = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330"
}

reader "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org" { password_file = "etc/authnd/reader.pw" }

user "alice" {
 password_file = "etc/authnd/alice.pw"
 attributes = { uidNumber = "1000", gidNumber = "1000", homeDirectory = "/home/alice" }
}

user "bob" {
 nt_hash = "8846F7EAEE8FB117AD06BDD830B7586C"
 attributes = { sambaSID = "S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-1104" }
}

user "carol" { password = "carol-pw" }
$ authnd check ldaps
ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, posixAccount, sambaSamAccount, uidObject uid, cn, gidNumber, homeDirectory, uidNumber, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, sambaSamAccount, uidObject uid, cn, sambaSID and sambaNTPassword
carol the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, sambaSamAccount, uidObject
carol has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
carol is published without sambaNTPassword: no sambaSID and no uidNumber to derive one from
a bind carries a password
bob cannot bind with a password: the source holds only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is published over TLS: it IS the credential, and whoever reads it authenticates as that person over NTLMv2
in sambaSamAccount, with sambaSIDs in S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330 (a person's own sambaSID, or RID 2 x uidNumber + 1000)
this configuration can be served

and, for the StartTLS listener, sambaNTPassword is published over TLS, once StartTLS has been asked for. alice has no NT hash written down; theirs is derived from the password they have. bob’s hash is published for an SMB server to use, and check says, too, that bob cannot bind to authnd itself. carol’s entry is published without the attribute, and an SMB server cannot serve carol until a source gives them a uidNumber or a sambaSID.

What a reader is given, over the StartTLS listener of the same people:

$ LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never ldapsearch -ZZ -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=alice)'
dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: top
objectClass: account
objectClass: posixAccount
objectClass: sambaSamAccount
objectClass: uidObject
uid: alice
cn: alice
gidNumber: 1000
homeDirectory: /home/alice
uidNumber: 1000
sambaSID: S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-3000
sambaNTPassword: D061EF15E9494B458016FA760CECDD63

Only a reader can search, so only a reader ever sees the attribute. Who may read it is therefore the same question as who holds a reader’s password.

NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and nothing else will do

A file server asking authnd about somebody can serve them over SMB only if the source held enough for that: a password, or the hash. A person who comes from a directory that only checks passwords — a password check in check — can never be given a sambaNTPassword, whatever authnd does in between. Without publish_nt_hash, nobody can: check then says sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session.

Tokens need it too

An oidc block refuses a token over a connection that is not encrypted, unless allow_plaintext = true says that TLS is terminated in front of this process.

item.title: A person changing their own password
item.description:
A person may change their own password, and nobody else’s, through the RFC 3062 password modify operation (what ldappasswd sends) or an RFC 4511 modify. In both, the current password must be sent with the new one, whatever the connection bound with. A session bound with an OAUTHBEARER token — short-lived, and possibly one factor — could otherwise turn it into a permanent password that also works for kinit.

This is OpenLDAP’s ppolicy behaviour with pwdSafeModify set, with the result codes its ppolicy.c returns. RFC 3062 §3 allows it: “If oldPasswd is not present, the server MAY use other policy to determine whether or not to change the password.”

With ldappasswd

-t is a file holding the old password, -T one holding the new; -A and -S prompt for them instead.

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -T alice.new
Result: Insufficient access (50)
Additional info: a password change must send the old password with the new one
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t wrong.pwin -T alice.new
Result: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
Additional info: the old password sent is not the current one
$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.new
dn:uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org

The old password stops working at once, for a bind and — with a realm — for kinit. The server says so in its output:

alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password
alice changed their own password

authnd does not generate a password: a request without a new one is refused with unwillingToPerform (this server does not generate passwords: send the one you want). A password it invented would have to be sent back over the connection, and the one place it is certain to end up is a terminal’s scrollback.

With ldapmodify

The change is a delete of the old value followed by an add of the new one, in one request. RFC 4511 §4.6 applies a modify’s changes in order and atomically, so the delete — and the whole request with it — fails unless the value deleted is the one held:

dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
changetype: modify
delete: userPassword
userPassword: alice-test-pw
-
add: userPassword
userPassword: alice-new-pw
-

A bare replace proves nothing, and anything but userPassword is not something this server changes:

$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f replace.ldif
ldap_modify: Insufficient access (50)
additional info: a password change must send the old password with the new one
modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f other.ldif
ldap_modify: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
additional info: this server changes userPassword and nothing else, not cn
modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"

A modify that asks for a password and something else is refused whole: a modify is atomic, and honouring half of it would report success for something nobody asked for.

Who can change what

request answer
no old password, or a bare replace: userPassword insufficientAccessRights
an old password that is not the current one unwillingToPerform
somebody else’s entry insufficientAccessRights, a password may be changed only by the person it belongs to
an anonymous connection insufficientAccessRights, an anonymous connection has not said who it is
somebody with no password at all — they can only have bound with a token unwillingToPerform: a bearer token is not a password, and does not set the first one. An administrator sets it in the configuration
somebody served from a users block unwillingToPerform: authnd reads those sources and does not write them
the file cannot be written other (80), the password could not be written; the reason is in the server’s output

The second-to-last, from the release binary, for dora, who comes from a SQLite database:

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pwin -t dora.pwin -T dora.new
Result: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
Additional info: dora is served from a sqlite database, which this server reads and does not write

The person is matched by identity, not by DN: the session’s own name must be exactly the target’s, byte for byte, so a session bound as uid=Backup cannot change backup’s password even though the two DNs compare equal. That and the refusal of names that differ only by case are two controls that do not depend on each other.

Where the new password is written

Back into the file that declares the person, and nowhere else:

  • a user block with password_file has that file rewritten, keeping its owner and group where the process may, and its mode narrowed to at most 0600 — never widened;
  • a user block with password inline has the configuration file rewritten with the new value, keeping its comments, order and mode;
  • a user block with only an nt_hash is not given a password: that would change what can prove them, which is a change to the configuration.

Every write goes to a temporary file in the same directory, then a rename — so a full disk or a crash leaves the old password, not an empty file. That needs write access to the directory. Under the packaged unit, ProtectSystem=strict takes it away, and a change is refused like this:

$ ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -f safe.ldif
ldap_modify: Other (e.g., implementation specific) error (80)
additional info: the password could not be written
modifying entry "uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"

with the reason in the server’s output:

changing the password for alice: etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw: open etc/authnd/passwords/.hcldir-863420940: permission denied

So keep the passwords in a directory of their own, writable by the service, and the configuration read-only to it — the ReadWritePaths= drop-in. A person whose password is written inline would need /etc/authnd itself writable, which would also let the service rewrite its own configuration.

After a successful write, the configuration files are read again for the user blocks only: an unrelated edit waiting on disk does not take effect halfway because somebody changed a password. Everything else still waits for a restart. The files are still read whole, though, so if one of them no longer loads, the password is written and the client is told the password was written but this server did not reload it — the running server keeps the old one until it is restarted.

item.title: A Kerberos realm for the same people
item.description:
kerberos {
 realm = "EXAMPLE.ORG" # required, upper case
 keytab = "/etc/authnd/krb5.keytab" # required; must hold krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG
 listen = "127.0.0.1:88" # the default; UDP and TCP both
 lifetime = "10h" # the default, MIT's
}

A kerberos block makes authnd a KDC as well as a directory, through go-authn/kdc: the same people are issued tickets instead of only being looked up. It answers on UDP and TCP at the same address, requires encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication, and issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 tickets only. lifetime is a Go duration ("10h", "90m"). The directory and the realm are equals: if either stops, the process stops, because a server that kept answering LDAP after its KDC died would look healthy to everything that does not speak Kerberos.

Refused at startup:

$ authnd check cases/realm-lower.hcl
authnd: kerberos: realm "example.org" is not upper case: clients uppercase the realm they derive from a domain, and would then ask for a realm this server does not answer for

and likewise a realm with no name, no keytab, an address that does not parse, a lifetime Go cannot read, and a kerberos block beside an mfa block (below).

The keytab

The keytab holds the key authnd signs its own tickets with — krbtgt/REALM@REALM — and one key per service it issues tickets to. It is the same file those services read. The krbtgt password is never typed again, so make it random. With MIT’s ktutil (package krb5-user on Debian and Ubuntu; this recipe is the one docs/install.md gives, and was not run for these pages):

printf 'addent -password -p krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG -k 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96\n%s\nwkt /tmp/krb5.keytab\nquit\n' \
 "$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" | ktutil
sudo install -o root -g authnd -m 0640 /tmp/krb5.keytab /etc/authnd/krb5.keytab
rm /tmp/krb5.keytab

Add a service’s key the same way (-p nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG), and give that service the same key in its own keytab. On macOS, Heimdal’s ktutil -k <file> add -r -p <principal> -V 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 writes a random key without a password at all. Either way, read the keytab back before starting (klist -k with MIT, ktutil -k <file> list with Heimdal):

$ ktutil -k etc/authnd/krb5.keytab list
etc/authnd/krb5.keytab:
Vno Type Principal Aliases
1 aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG

A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused by check and at start; see check. The keytab is read once, at start: replacing it takes a restart.

Who can be issued a ticket

A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so it needs the person’s password, not only a way to check one. check says who can and who cannot, with the reason:

$ authnd check realm
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid
dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
staff alice and bob groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp), keytab etc/authnd/krb5.keytab
can be issued a ticket: alice and dora
CANNOT, whatever they type: bob and eli
a KDC must decrypt the pre-authentication with the person's key
bob and eli: an NT hash is only the RC4-HMAC key (RFC 4757), and this realm issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 alone, whose key is derived from the password itself
a bind carries a password
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served
the source has a ticket
a password (password, password_file, a SQL password column) yes
only an NT hash no: it is the RC4-HMAC key, and this realm issues AES only
only a password check (a users "ldap" directory behind this one) no: a source that only verifies a password cannot produce any key

For a directory behind this one, the last line of the realm part reads alice, bob, dora and eli: the source only verifies a password, so it cannot produce any key. That is structural rather than a matter of configuration, and finding it in check beats finding it from somebody whose kinit says their correct password is wrong.

kinit against it

A krb5.conf that names this KDC. ⛔ For MIT Kerberos the braces go on their own lines: its parser silently ignores a realm written on one line.

[libdefaults]
 default_realm = EXAMPLE.ORG
 dns_lookup_kdc = false
[realms]
 EXAMPLE.ORG = {
 kdc = 127.0.0.1:18388
 }

The same configuration served, and asked by macOS’s Heimdal kinit (--password-file reads the password from a file):

$ authnd --config realm
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database
realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp)
$ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:ccache
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 18 16:10:19 2026 Oct 19 02:10:19 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ kinit --password-file=wrong.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=bob.pwin bob@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal
$ kinit --password-file=dora.pwin zed@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm

The ticket lasts the default ten hours. bob typed the password their NT hash was computed from, and is still refused: the realm has no key for them. The KDC writes what it refused, with the Kerberos error code, to its output:

kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
kerberos: the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal (code 9)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6)

Pre-authentication required is the normal first round of a kinit: the client asks without pre-authentication and is told it is required, then asks again with it. alice’s successful kinit leaves only that line.

The realm says which names exist; the directory does not

An LDAP bind for a name nobody has is answered invalidCredentials, the same as a wrong password. The KDC answers no such principal in this realm (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN, code 6), as Kerberos KDCs do. With a kerberos block on an address others can reach, the list of names is therefore as guessable as it is from any KDC; listen defaults to loopback.

A password changed over LDAP

The KDC reads the same people the directory serves, so a password changed over LDAP reaches the realm at once — the old one stops working for kinit the moment it stops working for a bind:

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new
$ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=alice.new alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
$

Not beside an mfa block 

$ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl
authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks

RFC 4120’s encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication is keyed by the password alone. A second factor needs OTP pre-authentication (RFC 6560) inside FAST (RFC 6113), which this KDC does not implement. A realm here would hand out tickets on one factor to the people the mfa block says need two, and a ticket opens everything a bind does — so the choice is made closed: one or the other.

Ports

88 is privileged. Under the packaged unit, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE covers it; a server run as an ordinary user wants a high port, as above, and a krb5.conf that names it.

item.title: A second factor, over a protocol with one field
item.description:
