LDAP’s simple bind carries a name and a password and nothing else — no place for a code, no round trip to ask for one, and a client that speaks LDAP will not learn one. So the code goes on the end of the password, which is what appliances that do this do, and what people already know how to type:

password: hunter2314159
^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^
password the six digits on their phone
mfa {
 factors = 2
 distinct_kinds = true # two things they KNOW are not two factors
 # digits = 6, period = 30 (seconds) and window = 1 are the defaults
}

user "tess" {
 password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/tess.pw"
 totp_secret = "JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXPJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP" # ⛔ this IS the second factor
}
key default
factors 2 1 is refused (a password and nothing else: remove the block, or ask for 2); above 2 is refused, since a bind carries a password and a code and no third thing
distinct_kinds false the factors must be of different kinds — what “two-factor” is normally taken to mean
digits 6 6 to 10 (RFC 4226)
period 30 seconds one code lasts
window 1 steps either side of now that are accepted, for clocks that differ. Each step is a step of somebody else’s guessing time: set it on purpose
readers false whether readers carry a code too. A service account has no phone; one that does gets a totp_secret in its reader block

The secret can equally come from a database column (the fifth) or an LDAP attribute (totp_attribute); see people. A totp_secret in a user or reader block under 128 bits (RFC 4226 R6) stops the server, naming the person, rather than failing every one of their logins later:

$ authnd check cases/shorttotp.hcl
authnd: user "alice": totp_secret is 80 bits, and RFC 4226 requires at least 128: enrol again with a longer secret

Who cannot bind under it 

$ authnd check mfa
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds
alice has no second factor here, and cannot bind while one is required
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

That is the question to ask before turning the block on.

What the binds look like

The same configuration served, tess’s code computed from their secret at the moment of the bind:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.only
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.both
dn:uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.both
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=tess,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y tess.badcode
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.code
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)
$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org -y reader.pwin
dn:cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org

tess.only is tess’s password with no code; tess.both the same password and the current code, sent twice; tess.badcode that password and 000000; alice.code alice’s password and six digits. The client is told one thing — invalid credentials — whichever half was wrong: which one is a fact about the account, and telling somebody who has proved nothing narrows their next guess. The server’s own output says which:

tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 0 answered: your password (knowledge): directory: wrong password; your authenticator app (possession): not looked at, since the password in front of it was wrong
tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code has already been used
tess was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): totp: that code is not right
alice was refused: mfa: 2 factor(s) needed, 1 answered: your authenticator app (possession): not available
your authenticator app: mfa: this factor cannot be asked here: totp: nobody enrolled an authenticator for this person

What follows from the one field

  • The split is by length. The last digits characters are the code. A password ending in digits is fine — that is why tess’s password alone was read as a wrong password followed by a code. A field no longer than a code is refused rather than guessed at, because a short password cannot be told apart from one.
  • Both halves are always checked. Returning early on a wrong password would say, in the time taken, which half was wrong.
  • A code is used once. It is valid for a whole step, so a server that accepts one twice accepts a replay; every step up to the last accepted one is refused, not merely the same one.
  • Guessing is limited per name, with go-authn/totp’s defaults: after five wrong codes in a row a person is refused for fifteen minutes, the right code included, and after a hundred they are locked out until authnd restarts. The counts are kept in memory, per process.
  • Only a code behind the right password is counted: otherwise anybody who knew a name could freeze its owner with five binds. Behind a wrong password the code is still computed, against nothing that remembers — the first line of the output above, not looked at.
  • A reader is counted under its DN as the configuration spells it, so CN=Reader gets no fresh budget of its own.
  • Nobody enrolled is not a wrong code. A person with no secret has answered nothing rather than answered wrongly, and the server’s output says nobody enrolled an authenticator for this person.

Not with a realm

A kerberos block and an mfa block in one configuration are refused: a kinit proves the password and nothing else, and this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication. See the realm.

Tokens, under the same policy

A token at the bind, with an oidc block, is counted by what its issuer says it checked — the amr claim. A token with no amr is one factor, and this policy refuses it.

item.title: A token at the bind, in a field that is not the password
item.description:
go-authn/oidc verifies a token into an identity. The obvious way to carry one to an LDAP server is the password field, and it works once and then stops: the password field is where the mfa block takes the code off the end, and a token cannot be both.

So the token goes where the protocol has a place for it. A SASL bind’s credentials are an octet string of the mechanism’s own shape, and RFC 7628’s OAUTHBEARER shape is a GS2 header followed by key/value pairs, one of which is auth=Bearer <token>:

n,,^Aauth=Bearer eyJ…^A^A

The password field is left alone. On one listener, at the same time, a person can type a password with a code on the end and another can send a token.

oidc {
 issuer = "https://login.example.org/realms/staff" # the "iss" a token must carry, and where discovery starts
 audience = "ldap" # this server's client id at the provider

 # username_claim = "preferred_username" which claim names the person here
 # jwks_url = "…" skips discovery, for a provider that does not publish it
 # allow_plaintext = true only when TLS is terminated in front of this process
}

issuer and audience are required. Without username_claim, the name is preferred_username, then email when email_verified is true, then sub. With the block, the root DSE advertises the mechanism:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' supportedSASLMechanisms
dn:
supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER

Without it, every SASL bind is answered authMethodNotSupported — not this way, which sends a client somewhere different from wrong password.

Discovery happens at startup

The provider’s discovery document and keys are read when the server starts, and by check. A provider that cannot be reached stops the server where somebody is watching, rather than refusing every bind later:

$ authnd check cases/oidc.hcl
authnd: oidc "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff": oidc: reading https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration: Get "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

An issuer that is not https is refused, except on loopback:

$ authnd check cases/oidc-http.hcl
authnd: oidc "http://login.example.org/realms/staff": oidc: http://login.example.org/realms/staff is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way

How many factors is a token?

Whatever the issuer says it checked, and nothing more. A token carries RFC 8176’s amr, the methods the provider used. That is the only evidence there is, so it is what the mfa policy counts, by kind:

amr method kind
pwd, pin, kba, mca knowledge
otp, hwk, swk, sms, tel, sc, pop, user, wia, mfa possession
fpt, face, iris, retina, vbm, geo inherence
anything else unknown, which never satisfies distinct_kinds
no amr at all one factor, possession — the token itself

Two methods of one kind are one factor. The alternative would be this server inventing a second factor nobody performed; and a server that believes the issuer about who this is has no separate ground for disbelieving it about how it checked.

With an mfa block, check says it:

$ authnd check sasl
ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds
or a token from http://127.0.0.1:18481, over SASL OAUTHBEARER over TLS
a token counts for the factors its amr claim names, so one with no amr is refused by this policy
alice has no second factor here, so a password cannot satisfy this policy; a token whose amr names two kinds still can
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

alice has no totp_secret, so a password with a code can never be enough for them; a token whose amr names two kinds can, as the first bind below shows.

What the binds look like

The issuer here is a small test provider on loopback, and oidctool a test client written for these pages: it signs a token for the name given, with the amr given, sends it in an OAUTHBEARER bind (with an authzid when a fifth argument names one), and prints the bind’s result code and the server’s SASL credentials. Against the configuration above, over ldaps://:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 0, serverSaslCreds
$ ./oidctool alice '' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","kba"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls tess
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"insufficient_scope","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}
$ ./oidctool zed '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"invalid_token","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}

0 is success, 49 invalidCredentials, 14 saslBindInProgress. A ["pwd","kba"] token names two methods of one kind, so it counts once. And to the same configuration without cert_file and key_file, on a plaintext listener:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3893 clear
bind result 13

13 is confidentialityRequired: a token is not taken over a connection that is not encrypted.

What the server wrote for the four binds over ldaps:// that were refused:

alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: the token is for "alice" and asks to act as "tess"; this server does not delegate
zed was refused: the token verified, and no source here publishes anybody by that name

and for the plaintext one:

a token was refused: OAUTHBEARER was offered over a connection that is not encrypted, and allow_plaintext is not set

A successful OAUTHBEARER bind leaves the connection bound as uid=<name>,ou=people,<base_dn>, spelled as every other entry is.

What it refuses

  • A token in the clear. A bearer token needs no other half: whoever reads it off the wire is that person until it expires. allow_plaintext = true exists for a deployment that terminates TLS in front of this process, and check then says a token may cross this socket in the clear.
  • A request to be somebody else. The GS2 header may name an authzid. A token for alice carrying a request to act as tess is refused, not quietly treated as either.
  • A token for somebody no source here publishes. The client is told only invalid_token; which names exist is not something to hand out one guess at a time. The reason is in the server’s output.
  • Channel binding. A GS2 header with p= — the client insists on channel binding — is refused: this server does not do it, and accepting the header while binding nothing would let the client believe the channel was checked.
  • A mechanism this server does not speak, with authMethodNotSupported.

A refusal of the token itself is RFC 7628 §3.2.3’s: a JSON error carrying openid-configuration, returned as saslBindInProgress so the client can send the ^A that ends the exchange. A token that verifies but does not satisfy the mfa policy is answered plainly invalidCredentials, as the second and third binds above show.

A token does not set a password

A person who has only ever signed in with a token cannot use that session to give themselves a first password, and a person who has one must still send it to change it. See changing a password.

item.title: Running it: signals, restarts and what it says
item.description:
It reads everything once

The configuration files, every source behind them, the TLS certificate and the keytab are read at start. There is no reload, and the packaged unit has no ExecReload=. After changing any of them:

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd
sudo systemctl restart authnd

The one thing applied while it runs is a password a person changes through authnd, which re-reads the user blocks and nothing else.

Signals

signal what happens
SIGTERM, SIGINT it prints stopping, closes the listeners and every established connection, stops the realm, closes the sources, and exits 0 once the server has really finished
SIGHUP it is caught and logged, and authnd stays up without reloading anything 
$ authnd --config etc/authnd
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database
hangup: authnd does not reload; restart it to apply a changed configuration, certificate or keytab
alice's password change was refused: the old password did not verify: directory: wrong password
alice changed their own password
stopping

That is one run: a kill -HUP, two attempts to change a password (the first refused, the second accepted), then a kill -TERM. The process was still there after the SIGHUP.

A SIGHUP used to kill authnd — Go’s default for a signal nobody handles — and systemd counts death by SIGHUP as a clean exit, so Restart=on-failure did not start it again: one kill -HUP or one logrotate postrotate took a directory down for good. It is caught now so that the habit is harmless, and the line says what to do instead.

Closing established connections, not only the listener, is deliberate: a server that stopped accepting and left its open connections answering would look stopped and not be, which is the restart that does not take.

What it writes

Everything goes to standard output, which under systemd is the journal (journalctl -u authnd):

  • at start, where it listens and whom it serves — ldap on …, ldaps on … or ldap+starttls on …, then realm EXAMPLE.ORG on … (udp and tcp) with a kerberos block;
  • every refused bind under an mfa block, every refused token, every refused or completed password change, with the reason — which the client is never told; see the second factor and tokens;
  • every request the KDC refuses, prefixed kerberos:, with the Kerberos error code; see the realm;
  • the LDAP library’s own log, in slog text form, at level info.

A plain wrong password on a simple bind, with no mfa block, is answered invalidCredentials and not logged by authnd itself.

When it does not start

A refusal is one line on standard error, prefixed authnd:, and exit status 1; under the unit, Restart=on-failure then tries again every five seconds and the line is in the journal each time. Everything check refuses is refused here too, and the one thing only the server finds is an address it cannot listen on — see check. The LDAP listener, the certificate and the realm are all opened before the first line is printed, so a server that cannot start prints only the refusal. Here a second instance meets the first one’s Kerberos port:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

The ldap on … line, and realm … on … after it, mean both halves are listening.

Telling that it is up

There is no health endpoint and no metrics. What there is:

  • the process and its exit status — under systemd, systemctl is-active authnd. If the LDAP listener or the realm stops of its own accord, the whole process ends with that error, so a live process is one whose two halves both answer;
  • the root DSE, which answers an anonymous client and says which version it is talking to:
$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' '+' '*'
dn:
objectClass: top
objectClass: OpenLDAProotDSE
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.1
supportedControl: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.1
supportedControl: 1.3.6.1.1.13.2
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1
supportedFeatures: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.3
subschemaSubentry: cn=Subschema
vendorName: go-authn/authnd
vendorVersion: v0.11.1

On a StartTLS listener that query needs -ZZ. A probe that proves more — that a source still answers — is a bind as a person or a reader kept for the purpose; with a users "ldap" block, that bind reaches the directory behind this one.

What lives where, and what a restart loses

configuration, passwords, DSN, certificate, keytab the files the configuration names; nothing is copied
a SQLite database wherever its DSN says; /var/lib/authnd under the unit
second-factor counts and lockouts memory only: a restart forgets them, including a person locked out after a hundred wrong codes
used one-time codes memory only
